title: How Traditional Diets Shape Unique Gut Microbes in India's Tribal Communities
excerpt: A growing body of research shows that India's indigenous populations harbor some of the most diverse gut microbiomes on Earth — and that those microbes disappear rapidly when diets westernize.
body:
• Indian tribal communities following traditional diets harbor significantly greater gut microbial diversity than urban populations, with unique bacteria specialized for fiber and plant-based food digestion
  • Prevotella — a genus linked to breaking down complex plant carbohydrates — is the most abundant gut bacteria in traditional Indian diets, from Kerala to Madhya Pradesh to Himalayan foothills
  • Research on Indo-Canadians found their gut microbiomes shift dramatically as diets westernize, with ultra-processed foods making up over 60% of daily calories compared to 12% for Indians in India
  • IBD incidence among South Asians in Canada is more than six times higher than in India, a gap researchers link to dietary acculturation and microbiome disruption

India's tribal and indigenous communities may hold a biological blueprint for gut health that the modern world is rapidly losing. A growing body of research — spanning populations from Tamil Nadu to the Himalayan foothills to the Indian diaspora in Canada — is revealing how traditional diets cultivate uniquely diverse gut microbiomes, and how quickly those microbial ecosystems collapse when people adopt westernized eating patterns.

What Makes Tribal Gut Microbiomes Different

Tribal populations across India maintain gut microbiota with significantly greater taxonomic diversity and functional richness than their urban counterparts. This is largely attributable to traditional diets that are high in fiber, fermented foods, and locally sourced ingredients, with minimal consumption of ultra-processed foods.

A 2026 study published in Frontiers in Pharmacology examined the gut microbiota of the Mulluvadi tribal community in Tamil Nadu, finding that their microbiomes were enriched with fiber-degrading and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria — microbes that play critical roles in immune regulation, metabolism, and protection against inflammatory diseases. The researchers noted that such strains are increasingly absent in urban Indian populations.

Earlier research from the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) in Bhopal, published in Nature, compared gut microbes from populations in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh with contrasting diets. The Kerala group consumed rice, meat, and fish; the Madhya Pradesh group ate primarily wheat, dairy, and plant-based foods. Despite these dietary differences, both populations were enriched in Prevotella — a genus specialized in breaking down complex plant carbohydrates — along with Mitsuokella, Lactobacillus, and Megasphaera species found in far higher abundance in Indians than in populations elsewhere in the world.

Diet Transitions and Microbiome Shifts

A landmark Stanford University study examined four closely related populations in the Himalayan foothills — the Tharu, Raute, Raji, and Chepang — who share ancestry, language, and cultural practices but differ in how long ago they transitioned from hunter-gatherer to agricultural lifestyles. The Chepang still forage; the Tharu have practiced agriculture for 250 to 300 years. The Raute and Raji shifted within the last 30 to 40 years.

"This study indicates that human microbiomes may have changed gradually as human lifestyle changed, and those changes can happen within a human's lifetime."

— Aashish Jha, postdoctoral researcher, Stanford University

The findings, published in PLOS Biology, showed that gut microbiome composition diverged in direct proportion to each group's agricultural dependence. The more time since the transition from foraging, the more the microbiome resembled that of industrial populations — with fewer of the fiber-processing bacteria found in hunter-gatherer communities.

What This Means for the Diaspora

The implications extend well beyond tribal communities. A 2025 study led by the University of British Columbia compared gut microbiomes across more than 170 participants in India and Canada — including Indians living in India, first-generation Indian immigrants, and Indo-Canadians born in Canada.

The results were stark. Indians in India maintained gut bacteria dominated by Prevotella, linked to high-fiber, plant-based diets. Indo-Canadians showed a "transitional" microbiome — depleted of beneficial Prevotella and increasingly colonized by bacteria common in western populations, such as Blautia and Anaerostipes.

The dietary data underscored the shift: ultra-processed foods made up more than 60% of Indo-Canadians' daily calories, compared to just 12% for Indians living in India. Fiber intake was highest in India and lowest among Indo-Canadians.

The health consequences are measurable. IBD incidence among South Asians in Canada is more than six times higher than in India — a gap researchers attribute to dietary acculturation.

"Our study shows that the gut doesn't just adapt to where you live, it adapts to what you eat. For Indo-Canadians, that means a microbiome caught between two worlds."

— Dr. Deanna Gibson, Professor of Biology, UBC Okanagan

Protecting a Biological Heritage

Researchers warn that the rapid industrialization of food systems in India itself threatens to replicate the same microbiome disruption seen in immigrant populations. IBD rates in India have risen sharply in recent years, a trend scientists link directly to the westernization of Indian diets.

India's tribal communities, with their diverse traditional food systems, represent a living archive of microbial diversity that has co-evolved with human diets over centuries. Understanding and preserving that diversity is not just an academic exercise — it may hold clues to preventing the chronic inflammatory and metabolic diseases increasingly common in both India and its diaspora abroad.
